gallery.title: File:Colonel Joseph Martin Greenwood.jpeg
gallery.description: View of 'Greenwood,' a two-story Flemish-bond brick house built for Colonel Joseph Martin, son of General Joseph Martin. The house was built in 1808–1810 at Axton, Henry County, Virginia, for Col. Martin, who was born in 1785 and served in the War of 1812. Col. Martin served in both the Virginia House of Delegates and for eight years in the Virginia Senate. He also served as a member of the constitutional convention of 1829–1830, and three times as a presidential elector. He was lifelong friends with Archibald Stuart of Patrick County, Virginia, father of Confederate general J.E.B. Stuart, as well as with United States President and Virginia native John Tyler. During the War of 1812, Col. Martin commanded a regiment of militia. His plantation house, Greenwood, is based on a symmetrical three-bay Early Republic style and has a centered single-leaf wood door with a full surround. The house's portico is supported by paired Ionic columns. The windows are 9/9 sash windows with splayed brick lintels. The home features two exterior-end chimneys with disengaged stacks. It has seven fireplaces. In about 1940, basement excavations caused a cave-in, and the house was disassembled and moved from its location at Axton in Henry County to nearby Martinsville, named for Col. Joseph Martin's father. Col. Joseph Martin married Sally (Hughes) Martin, daughter of Col. Archelaus Hughes of Hughesville, Patrick County, Virginia, and a noted Revolutionary War soldier and patriot. Col. Martin and Sally Hughes Martin had eight daughters and four sons. Of the 12 children, two married members of the Hairston family; two married members of the Pannill family; and another two married members of the Dillard family. [1] An oil-on-canvas portrait believed to be Col. Joseph Martin is in the collection of the Bassett Historical Center, Bassett, Virginia. Also surviving is the porcelain dinnerware service from Col. Martin's home 'Greenwood,' manufactured by John Ridgway & Co., Staffordshire.

gallery.source: Patrick Henry's Leatherwood Home Henry County Virginia
gallery.description: Virginia state historic marker near the location of patriot and Virginia governor Patrick Henry's Leatherwood plantation, which eventually encompassed over 10,000 acres in what later became Henry County, named for him. Henry lived on his Leatherwood plantation, near his friend General Joseph Martin, from 1779 to 1784. In that year he moved to Chesterfield County, Virginia.

gallery.filename: Peter Wilson Watkins by James Westhall Ford.jpg
gallery.title: File:Peter Wilson Watkins by James Westhall Ford.jpg
gallery.description: Portrait of Peter Wilson Watkins, oil on canvas (mounted on board), by the American artist James Westhall Ford (1805-1866). Undated. 43 in. x 28 1/2 in. Peter Watkins Wilson was born in 1816, married Louisa Hardyman Hairston in 1844, and lived at Shawnee Plantation in Henry County, Virginia. He died 17 February 1890. Private collection. Image courtesy of the Tennessee Portrait Project.

gallery.filename: George 'Old Rusty' Hairston by James Westhall Ford 1858.gif
gallery.title: File:George 'Old Rusty' Hairston by James Westhall Ford 1858.gif
gallery.description: Portrait of George Hairston II, known as 'Old Rusty,' by the American painter James Westhall Ford, dated 1858. George Hairston II graduated from Princeton in 1805 and married Louisa Hardyman, who was a ward of President John Tyler. Hairston first lived at Marrowbone Plantation in Henry County, but later built Hordsville Plantation house, on the site owned earlier (and named for) Mordecai Hord. Hairston served in the Virginia legislature, and was a founder of the Smith River Navigation Company and the Union Iron Works. He is buried at Hordsville. Private collection. Image courtesy of the Tennessee Portrait Project.
